signals.headline: Roman will study the universe as a population
signals.canonicalClaim: NASA launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on August 30, 2026, beginning a roughly three-month deployment, calibration, and commissioning period before planned first science images in early 2027.
knownFacts: Reuters independently reported the launch from Kennedy Space Center at 7:26 a.m. EDT.
NASA described a 300-megapixel infrared camera with a field at least 100 times larger than Hubble at comparable sharpness.
NASA planned processed observations without a proprietary period.
uncertainties: Launch success did not establish successful deployment, commissioning, instrument performance, survey yield, or long-term open-data impact.
Projected galaxy and exoplanet counts were mission expectations, not observed outcomes.

evidence.notes: NASA supplied mission specifications and milestones while Reuters independently reported the launch event.

sources.title: NASA launches Roman Space Telescope from Florida
Nine things to know about the Roman mission

openQuestions: Will all deployments and instrument calibrations succeed?
When will first science images and survey data be released?
Will immediate public access produce substantial research beyond the mission’s planned programs?

watchFor.trigger: NASA reports spacecraft or instrument deployment, anomaly, or calibration results.

watchFor.description: First science images and initial data release
watchFor.trigger: NASA releases the first processed observations.
Published results compare achieved field, sensitivity, cadence, and yield with mission expectations.

trackingTerms: Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope status

disposition.reason: The mission has a precise baseline, a sequence of near-term technical gates, and years of measurable scientific and institutional outcomes.

signals.selectionReason: Roman made field of view and open access part of the scientific argument, not merely conveniences around the instrument.

signals.headline: Coloratura makes sound carry the walls
signals.canonicalClaim: Nakama Game Studio described Coloratura as a free-moving 3D PlayStation 5 adventure designed to be navigable without sight through positional sound, objective audio, broad geometry, and blind playtesting.
knownFacts: The developer described positional sounds for discovered objects and a bell indicating the current objective.
The design reduced strict collisions and used broad walls to limit snagging on invisible furniture.
uncertainties: The finished public release had not yet tested navigation, comfort, cognition, hearing variation, or hardware dependence across a broad population of blind players.
The source was a promotional first-party design account.

evidence.notes: The design intentions are well specified but practical accessibility remains unverified until release and independent use.

sources.title: Coloratura: designing a world where sound is the only guide

openQuestions: How will blind players evaluate navigation and comfort in the released game?
How dependent is the experience on headphones, spatial-audio hardware, or particular hearing profiles?
Will post-release feedback produce design changes?

watchFor.description: A release date or playable public build
watchFor.trigger: The developer announces a date, demo, beta, or launch.
Blind reviewers and accessibility specialists document the finished experience.
Patches or developer notes respond to player accessibility findings.

disposition.reason: The project makes concrete, consequential accessibility claims with a clear future test by the people it intends to serve.

signals.selectionReason: It treated accessibility as a source of mechanics and spatial imagination rather than a translation layer added after visual design.

signals.headline: Sixty-six pieces change the name on an altarpiece

canonicalSubject.name: The Assumption of the Virgin by Andrea della Robbia and workshop
aliases: Met Assumption of the Virgin terracotta

signals.canonicalClaim: The Metropolitan Museum of Art displayed 33 conserved sections of a 66-part Florentine glazed-terracotta altarpiece and revised its attribution from Andrea della Robbia’s workshop to Andrea della Robbia and his workshop, circa 1485.
knownFacts: The object had been out of public view for almost seventy years.
The installation distinguished the surviving 33 sections from a graphic and three-dimensional reconstruction of the whole.
The revised attribution retained collective workshop authorship while assigning Andrea a more direct role.
uncertainties: The article did not identify a single decisive signature; the attribution depended on assembled material, stylistic, and workshop evidence.
Future scholarship could refine the reconstruction, dating, or division of labor.

evidence.notes: The museum’s press and collection records are primary sources for its conservation treatment, display, and attribution decision.

sources.title: The Assumption of the Virgin and digital reconstruction
Prudence and scholarship on glazed terracotta

openQuestions: Will the museum publish detailed technical evidence for the revised attribution?
Will outside specialists accept, refine, or contest the new wording?
Can additional fragments or documentation be identified?

watchFor.description: Technical publication or catalog documenting the conservation and attribution
watchFor.trigger: The Met publishes material analysis, join evidence, workshop comparisons, or a catalog.
External specialists cite, support, or challenge the revised attribution.

disposition.reason: The reattribution is a strong historical baseline, but meaningful changes are likely to be occasional scholarly developments rather than frequent updates.

signals.selectionReason: The broken and modular object made workshop collaboration harder to erase while keeping the boundary between surviving material and reconstruction visible.
